tagline: Born enslaved, the barber who founded Atlanta Life Insurance became Atlanta's wealthiest Black citizen
burial: Buried at South-View Cemetery. Reported by the Georgia Historical Society marker at the cemetery (erected 2016), which names "Alonzo Herndon, founder of the Atlanta Life Insurance Company" among its notable burials; Wikipedia's South-View list also includes him and his first wife, Adrienne McNeil Herndon.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Alonzo Franklin Herndon was born enslaved on June 26, 1858, in Walton County, Georgia, and grew up on a farm in Social Circle, about 40 miles east of Atlanta. His father, Frank Herndon, was a white man who enslaved him; his mother, Sophenie, was an enslaved woman. He had a younger brother, Thomas, known as Tom, and his maternal grandparents lived with the family after emancipation. After emancipation his father sent the family away, and at about age seven Alonzo, his mother, his brother and his grandparents were homeless and destitute. In 1893 Herndon married Adrienne Elizabeth McNeil, a professor at Atlanta University who had studied dramatic arts in Boston and New York and received the Belasco Gold Medal in 1908. Adrienne died in 1910 and, according to Wikipedia's South-View list, is also buried at South-View. Their only child, Norris Herndon, succeeded his father as chief executive of Atlanta Life and ran the company until his death in 1955. Herndon later married Jessie Gillespie of Chicago. After his death she joined the Atlanta Life board, and she and his stepson took control of the company as major stockholders.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Alonzo Herndon had only about one year of formal schooling before he left Social Circle, Georgia, in 1878. As a boy in the 1870s he worked instead, peddling peanuts, homemade molasses and axle grease to save money. According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, Herndon overcame illiteracy during his life. His practical education came through work: after leaving home he labored as a farmhand in Senoia, in Coweta County, where he began learning the barbering trade that would become the foundation of his later business success and of the insurance company he founded in 1905.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Alonzo Herndon left Social Circle on foot in 1878 with $11, worked as a farmhand in Senoia and learned barbering. He opened his first barbershop in Jonesboro, in Clayton County, and stayed about five years. In early 1883 he moved to Atlanta to work in William Dougherty Hutchins's barbershop on Marietta Street and bought a half interest in it about six months later. By 1904 he owned three Atlanta barbershops; the flagship at 66 Peachtree Street was advertised as the largest and best in the region. Secondary sources call that shop the "Crystal Palace" and describe gold fixtures, marble floors and crystal chandeliers, with Black barbers serving an exclusively white clientele. In 1905 Herndon bought a failing mutual aid association and incorporated it as the Atlanta Mutual Insurance Association, serving as president and chief stockholder. Its assets grew from $5,000 in 1905 to more than $400,000 by 1922, when it was reorganized as the Atlanta Life Insurance Company and gained legal reserve status, which only four other Black insurers then held. In the 1920s Atlanta Life expanded into Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Tennessee and Texas, and Herndon rescued failing Black businesses by reinsuring their policyholders. He owned more than 100 houses, commercial property on Auburn Avenue and an estate in Tavares, Florida.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Alonzo Herndon took part in two of the most important Black organizing efforts of the early twentieth century. In 1900 he was among the Atlanta delegates at the founding meeting of Booker T. Washington's National Negro Business League in Boston, and in 1905 he was one of the 29 men at the founding meeting of W. E. B. Du Bois's Niagara Movement. Herndon also experienced racial violence directly: in September 1906, during the Atlanta race massacre, a mob smashed the windows of his barbershop while he was at home, and Black barbers in a shop across the street were killed. Herndon supported many Atlanta institutions, including the YMCA, Atlanta University, the Leonard Street, Carrie Steele and Diana Pace orphanages, the Herndon Day Nursery, First Congregational Church, Atlanta State Savings Bank and the Southview Cemetery Association, the organization behind the cemetery where he is buried.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Alonzo Herndon died in Atlanta on July 21, 1927, a few weeks after his 69th birthday. His real estate was assessed at nearly $325,000, and the New Georgia Encyclopedia describes him as Atlanta's wealthiest Black citizen at his death. Atlanta Life survived into the 21st century and is regularly ranked by Black Enterprise among the top Black financial companies. The Herndon Home at 587 University Place NW, built in 1910 in the Classical Revival style with Beaux Arts influences, has much of its design credited to Adrienne Herndon, and African American craftsmen did almost all of the work except the electrical and plumbing. It was named an Atlanta Landmark Building on October 14, 1989, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places and designated a National Historic Landmark on February 16, 2000. The Alonzo F. and Norris B. Herndon Foundation has run it as a museum since 1983 and supports entrepreneurship, including the "Game Changer" program for 11th and 12th graders that began in 2013. In 2016 a Georgia Historical Society marker at South-View Cemetery named Herndon among its notable burials.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Alonzo Herndon left home at about age 20 with just $11 and became Atlanta's wealthiest Black citizen. A mob attacked his barbershop during the 1906 Atlanta race massacre. Herndon attended the founding meetings of both Booker T. Washington's National Negro Business League in 1900 and W. E. B. Du Bois's Niagara Movement in 1905. His 1905 insurance association grew from $5,000 to more than $400,000 in assets by 1922 and became Atlanta Life. His Herndon Home, built in 1910, is a National Historic Landmark and museum, and his first wife Adrienne, credited with much of its design, is also buried at South-View.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources describe Alonzo Herndon's wealth differently. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says he was Atlanta's wealthiest Black citizen at his death but does not call him a millionaire. Rough Draft Atlanta calls him Atlanta's first Black millionaire, and Wikipedia's South-View Cemetery list describes him as one of the first Black millionaires; these claims come from secondary sources and are not confirmed by the encyclopedia. Sources also differ on his famous barbershop. The New Georgia Encyclopedia places his flagship shop at 66 Peachtree Street by 1904 but never uses the name Crystal Palace. Secondary sources, including Edwardian Promenade and Rough Draft Atlanta, use that name, but they disagree on when the shop opened as the Crystal Palace: one gives 1902, while another says the Herndon barbershop had become the Crystal Palace by spring 1913. It has not been confirmed which source gives which date, so no opening year is stated here.

tagline: Atlanta Life president, Atlanta Inquirer co-founder, and civil rights leader who broke color barriers
burial: Buried at South-View Cemetery. Reported by Find a Grave (memorial 102285243) and by Wikipedia's South-View list, which cites Henderson's 2018 book South-View: An African American City of the Dead; the Georgia Historical Society marker at the cemetery does not name him.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Jesse Hill Jr. was born in St. Louis, Missouri, to Nancy Dennis Martin and Jesse Hill. Find a Grave and Wikipedia give his birth date as May 30, 1926, which fits his reported age of 86 at his death in December 2012; the New Georgia Encyclopedia gives his birth year as 1927. Hill served in the Korean War from 1952 to 1954. In 1955 he married Azira Gonzalez, and the couple had two daughters, Nancy Mercedes and Azira Dominga. Jesse Hill Jr. died on December 17, 2012, at age 86; Wikipedia gives Atlanta as the place of death. His funeral was held at Big Bethel AME Church, which stands at the corner of Auburn Avenue and the street that had been renamed Jesse Hill Jr. Drive in his honor.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Jesse Hill Jr. earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and physics from Lincoln University in Missouri in 1947. He then studied at the University of Michigan, where he received a graduate degree in 1949; the New Georgia Encyclopedia describes it as an MBA, while the Associated Press obituary calls it a master's in actuarial science. That training prepared Hill for a career as one of the few African American actuaries in the country. The University of Michigan later awarded Jesse Hill Jr. an honorary doctor of laws degree in the 1990s.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Jesse Hill Jr. moved to Atlanta in 1949 to join Atlanta Life Insurance Company as assistant actuary, one of the few African American actuaries in the country. Between 1949 and 1973 he rose to vice president and chief actuary. In 1973 Hill was elected president and CEO of Atlanta Life, the company's third president and the first not related to founder Alonzo Herndon. He retired from Atlanta Life in 1995, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, although other sources give different dates. In 1960 he helped create the Atlanta Inquirer, described by the Associated Press as the city's first newspaper for the African American community, and served as its publisher until 1985. Hill served on the boards of eight major corporations, including Knight Ridder, Delta Air Lines, National Service Industries and SunTrust Banks. He was a founding director of MARTA and served on the board for the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, which he helped bring to the city. He became head of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce in 1977, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, as its first African American leader. Hill is also credited with expanding African American access to affordable home mortgages in Georgia, Alabama, Texas and Florida.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Jesse Hill Jr. was deeply involved in Atlanta's civil rights movement. During the 1950s and 1960s he collected donations from Atlanta Life employees for Martin Luther King Jr.'s efforts, and the King Center described him as having a close relationship with King and helping ensure his legacy would be remembered. In 1960 Hill helped produce "A Second Look," a survey of Atlanta's Black population, with the Atlanta Committee for Cooperative Action. On the NAACP education committee he recruited students to desegregate Georgia colleges, which led to the admission of Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter to the University of Georgia. In the late 1960s and 1970s he led voter registration drives that added about 50,000 new Black voters in Atlanta, and he ran campaigns for Maynard Jackson, Atlanta's first Black mayor, and Andrew Young. From 1973 to 1984 Hill was the first African American member of the Georgia Board of Regents. He served on the board of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and chaired the King Center board from 1979 to 1993, according to the Associated Press. In 2003 he co-chaired the committee to rename Hartsfield International Airport for Maynard Jackson.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Jesse Hill Jr. was honored in his lifetime when Atlanta renamed Butler Street as Jesse Hill Jr. Drive in 2001. The street runs beside Big Bethel AME Church on Auburn Avenue, where his funeral was held in December 2012. In 2007 he received Atlanta Gas Light Company's Shining Light Award. Hill is credited with expanding African American access to affordable home mortgages in Georgia, Alabama, Texas and Florida, and with breaking color barriers as the first Black member of the Georgia Board of Regents and the first Black head of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce. His papers are held at the Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History in Atlanta, where researchers can study his business and civic career.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Jesse Hill Jr. was the first Atlanta Life president not related to founder Alonzo Herndon, who is buried in the same cemetery. Jesse Hill Jr. Drive, formerly Butler Street and renamed in 2001, runs beside Big Bethel AME Church, where his funeral was held. Hill co-founded the Atlanta Inquirer in 1960 and was its publisher until 1985. He recruited the students who desegregated the University of Georgia, Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter. He was also the first Black member of the Georgia Board of Regents, serving from 1973 to 1984.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources disagree on several details of Jesse Hill Jr.'s life. Birth year: the New Georgia Encyclopedia gives 1927, while Find a Grave and Wikipedia give May 30, 1926; his reported age of 86 at his December 2012 death fits 1926. Retirement from Atlanta Life: the New Georgia Encyclopedia says 1995, and the Auburn Avenue Research Library finding aid reportedly agrees; the Associated Press says 1990; Wikipedia says he served as CEO from 1973 to 1992. Atlanta Chamber of Commerce: the New Georgia Encyclopedia says he became chairman in 1977 and calls him the first African American elected president of a major-city chamber, while the Associated Press says he was named head in 1978 as its first Black president. Degrees: the New Georgia Encyclopedia places Lincoln University in St. Louis, while the Associated Press says Jefferson City, Missouri; the encyclopedia calls his 1949 Michigan degree an MBA, while the Associated Press calls it a master's in actuarial science. King Center: the Associated Press gives his board chairmanship as 1979 to 1993, while another AP version published by The Root reportedly ends it in 1995.

tagline: Built H.J. Russell & Company into a top minority-owned builder and quietly funded the civil rights movement
burial: Buried at South-View Cemetery. Reported by CBS News Atlanta (February 2, 2026), which notes "the burial site of Herman J. Russell, a major Atlanta developer" there, and by Wikipedia's South-View list, which cites Henderson's 2018 book on the cemetery.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Herman Jerome Russell was born on December 23, 1930, in Atlanta, the youngest of eight children of Maggie Googson and Rogers Russell, and grew up in the Summerhill neighborhood. As a child he overcame a severe speech impediment. In 1956 Russell married Otelia Hackney, a Clark College graduate from Union Point, Georgia, who died in 2006. Their children are Donata, H. Jerome and Michael; H. Jerome Russell is president of H.J. Russell & Company as of 2026. Russell later married Sylvia Anderson, described as a president at AT&T. In 2015, after his death, Joycelyn Darby Alston claimed to be his daughter, and DNA tests confirmed it; she declined a settlement, legal proceedings followed, and the family has not acknowledged her as an heir. Herman Russell died in Atlanta on November 15, 2014, at age 83, after what the Atlanta Black Star called a brief illness.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Herman J. Russell attended David T. Howard High School in Atlanta. While still a high school sophomore he bought his first piece of property, which he later developed to help pay for college. Russell went on to earn a degree in building construction from Tuskegee Institute, now Tuskegee University; the sources consulted do not give his graduation year. That construction training underpinned his later career, in which he took over his father's plastering business and built one of the largest minority-owned real estate and construction firms in the United States.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Herman J. Russell began his career in Atlanta in 1953, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, inherited his father's Rogers Russell Plastering Company in 1957, and had formed H.J. Russell Construction Company by the end of the 1960s. During the 1960s and 1970s he expanded into H.J. Russell and Company, H.J. Russell Plastering Company, Paradise Management Inc., DDR International and Southeast Land Development Company, later adding communications, concessions and sports franchises. In 1994 Russell reorganized his construction businesses under H.J. Russell and Company, with an estimated $150 million in annual sales and offices from Miami to New York. In the early 2000s the company was described as the largest minority business enterprise real estate firm in the United States. His firm worked on Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the Georgia Dome, Philips Arena (now State Farm Arena) and Turner Field, and was involved in building the new Falcons stadium, now Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The Atlanta Tribune also credits the company with work on the National Center for Civil and Human Rights and the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture. In 2004 Russell stepped down as CEO, handing leadership to his two sons and daughter, and remained board chairman. In 2014 he published his autobiography, Building Atlanta: How I Broke through Segregation to Launch a Business Empire.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Herman J. Russell was a friend of Martin Luther King Jr. and gave behind-the-scenes counsel and funding to the civil rights movement. According to the Atlanta Black Star, King relaxed at Russell's home and swam in his indoor pool, and Russell financed "a great portion" of the movement. In the early 1960s Russell became the first Black member of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, and he later became its second Black president. In 1973 he helped Maynard Jackson win election as Atlanta's first Black mayor. Russell served on the boards of Citizens Trust Bank, Central Atlanta Progress, the Butler Street YMCA, the Atlanta NAACP, Allen Temple AME Church and the Business Council of Georgia.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Herman J. Russell received the Horatio Alger Award in 1991. In 1999 he pledged $4 million for entrepreneurship education at Clark Atlanta University, Georgia State University, Morehouse College and Tuskegee. In 2009 the Russell family gave $1 million to Children's Healthcare of Atlanta at Hughes Spalding, whose lobby is named for Otelia and Herman Russell. He was named a Georgia Trustee in 2013 and received the Terrie M. Williams Inspiration Award in August 2014. Georgia State's Herman J. Russell Sr. International Center for Entrepreneurship bears his name. In 2019 the Russell Innovation Center for Entrepreneurs (RICE) opened in the renovated former company headquarters in Castleberry Hill, a building donated by the family; as of 2026 it reports serving 500 business leaders, helping create 2,500 jobs and generating more than $547 million in local economic activity. On April 29, 2026, the Georgia Historical Society unveiled a marker at the original headquarters at 504 Fair Street. Mayor Kasim Reed said in 2014, "He is one of the best men our city has ever produced."

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Herman J. Russell bought his first piece of property while still a high school sophomore. His firm helped build Hartsfield-Jackson airport, the Georgia Dome, Turner Field and Philips Arena. Martin Luther King Jr. relaxed at Russell's home and swam in his indoor pool, and Russell quietly helped fund the movement. He was the first Black member of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, in the early 1960s. His former headquarters is now the Russell Innovation Center for Entrepreneurs, opened in 2019, and received a Georgia Historical Society marker in 2026.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources give different founding dates for Herman J. Russell's company. The Atlanta Black Star says the company was founded in 1952. The Atlanta Tribune quotes his son H. Jerome Russell saying his father was 22 when he bought the land for the original building, which would be about 1952 or 1953, and describes the firm as nearly 75 years old in 2026. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says Russell began his career in Atlanta in 1953, inherited his father's Rogers Russell Plastering Company in 1957, and had formed H.J. Russell Construction Company by the end of the 1960s. These dates likely reflect different milestones, such as his early plastering and real estate work, inheriting his father's firm, and incorporating the general contracting company, rather than a single founding year.
